tur32-1: In BrAIST, the share of growing adolescents with 20–40 degree curves wearing a brace whose curve did not reach 50 degrees; 48% in those only observed
tur32-2: The size of scoliosis is measured with the Cobb angle on a standing full-spine X-ray. At each end of the curve, the vertebrae most tilted towards each other (the end vertebrae) are chosen; the angle between lines drawn along the upper surface of the upper end vertebra and the lower surface of the lower end vertebra is the size of the curve. A curve of 10 degrees or more is considered scoliosis.
tur32-3: In growing children, usually close observation. The international SOSORT guideline also recommends scoliosis-specific exercises at this stage; the SRS, however, states that the treatments shown to change the course of the curve are bracing and surgery.
tur32-4: In growing children a brace is usually recommended; between 20 and 25 degrees, the choice between observation and bracing depends on whether the curve is progressing and on remaining growth. SOSORT recommends continuing exercises alongside the brace.
tur32-5: The degree thresholds are taken from the SRS patient handbook and the exercise recommendations from the SOSORT guideline; the final decision rests with your doctor.
tur32-6: Risser signThe growth cartilage along the edge of the pelvic bone ossifies from the outer end inwards: there is no ossification at 0, it progresses from 1 to 4, and it fuses at 5. Grades 0–1 indicate more remaining growth.
tur32-7: More information: Radiopaedia, Cobb angle
tur32-8: Curves progress most during the rapid growth spurt of adolescence. The peak of the growth spurt comes earlier in girls than in boys; in girls, the period before the first period is the riskiest. So in young people going through the growth spurt (according to the SRS, usually between ages 10 and 15) a curve can increase even within a few months.
tur32-9: After growth ends, small curves usually progress little, while curves over 50 degrees usually continue to progress slowly in adulthood. In a Danish study in which patients treated with a brace or observation were followed for an average of 41 years, curves increased by an average of 0.2–0.5 degrees per year; even among curves under 25 degrees, some patients had an increase of more than 10 degrees, and the differences between individuals were large. In an approximately 50-year follow-up of untreated patients, shortness of breath was more common especially with very large curves (over 80 degrees) in the chest region.
tur32-10: In short: It has not been shown that one-sided habits cause scoliosis. Some studies found links with certain sitting habits; however, these links may also arise because the curve itself changes posture. Poor sitting and standing habits, on the other hand, have been linked to low back pain.
tur32-11: Scoliosis treatment has come a long way, from stretching tables to computer-designed braces and surgery that guides growth. Some methods were tried and abandoned; bracing and exercise have also been tested in randomised trials over the last 30 years, while surgical methods rely mostly on observational studies.
tur32-12: The Risser cast came into use; the Risser sign, which shows remaining growth, was published in 1958.
tur32-13: The Cotrel-Dubousset system was used for the first time, and three-dimensional correction of the spine became widespread in the following years; in the 1990s, pedicle screws began to be used in the thoracic vertebrae.
tur32-14: The BrAIST study, made up of randomised and preference groups, showed that bracing reduced progression of the curve to 50 degrees, the accepted threshold for surgery.
tur32-15: The international SOSORT guideline was updated; scoliosis-specific physiotherapy exercises and bracing were included as the main options for non-surgical treatment during growth.
tur32-16: In the USA, a vertebral body tethering device, which aims to correct the curve in growing children without fusing the spine, received limited approval under a Humanitarian Device Exemption (HDE), based on probable benefit rather than proven effectiveness.
tur32-17: Small curves (below about 25 degrees); in moderate curves, alongside a brace rather than on its own.
tur32-18: Growing young people with moderate curves (25–40 degrees); the doctor decides on the type of brace.
tur32-19: In CONTRAIS, success in preventing progression of more than 6 degrees was 76%, and 53% with physical activity alone. This rate cannot be compared with the success rate in BrAIST: the definitions of success and the patient groups differ, and the night brace was not compared directly with a full-time brace.
tur32-20: In BrAIST, the curve did not reach 50 degrees in 72% of those wearing a brace and 48% of those observed. The brace was prescribed for at least 18 hours a day; in those who actually wore it for an average of 13 hours or more a day, success was 90–93%.
tur32-21: It has to be worn for long hours; skin problems and a psychological burden can occur.
tur32-22: The most common operation; correction is usually partial. Movement is lost in the fused segment; there are risks of infection, bleeding and, rarely, nerve damage, and further surgery may be needed later.
tur32-23: Of the 57 patients on whom the approval was based, 43 avoided fusion at 2 years; problems such as cord breakage and overcorrection were reported. The data are short-term and uncontrolled; long-term results are not yet known.
tur32-24: The evidence is mixed. In a study of 45 adolescents in Türkiye, the group doing Schroth exercises in the clinic with a physiotherapist had a curve angle about 2.5 degrees smaller than the non-exercising group at 24 weeks (less than the measurement error), and their rib hump and waist asymmetry improved; the results of the group exercising alone at home were similar to those of the non-exercising group. The study is small and short. In the 2024 Cochrane review of 13 studies and 583 adolescents, the certainty of the evidence was mostly low or very low: compared with general exercise, scoliosis-specific exercises probably reduce trunk rotation (moderate certainty) and, when combined with a brace, may slightly reduce progression; differences in the angle stayed within the measurement error. In the CONTRAIS study of 135 adolescents in Sweden, scoliosis-specific exercise was no better than physical activity alone for moderate curves (success 58% versus 53%).
tur32-25: A high angle alone does not mean surgery. In 117 patients in the USA followed untreated for about 50 years, back pain was more common than in their peers, but their ability to carry out daily activities did not differ and their death rate was not increased; shortness of breath was more common especially with curves over 80 degrees in the chest region. Because curves over 50 degrees at the end of growth usually continue to progress slowly in adulthood, regular X-ray checks are needed even when surgery is not recommended. So the decision is made together with a spine surgeon, based on whether the curve is progressing, whether the trunk is balanced, pain, lung function and the person's expectations.
tur32-26: Have your child bend forward with feet together and knees straight, arms hanging freely. Looking from behind, check whether both sides of the back are at the same height. If there is a clear hump on one side, see a doctor. Even if the test looks normal, talk to your doctor if there is a clear difference in shoulder or waist level.
tur32-27: According to the SRS, children with scoliosis can do any sport unless they have back pain. The international guideline also recommends not giving up sport, even during brace treatment, because of its general health and psychological benefits; but no sport replaces treatment on its own. According to the same guideline, contact or highly dynamic sports should be done with caution during bracing; for young people at high risk of progression, talk to your doctor and physiotherapist about competitive sports that move the spine to extremes (for example rhythmic gymnastics). After surgery, your surgeon decides when you can return to sport.
tur32-28: There is no strong evidence for this: the Scoliosis Research Society (SRS) states that heavy bags and sport do not cause scoliosis or make a curve worse, and that poor posture does not cause scoliosis; a study of 966 students in Portugal also found no link between bag weight or postural habits and scoliosis. However, some studies based on school screening in China found links between scoliosis and sitting leaning to one side or slumped over the desk, and desks unsuited to the child's height; these studies do not show cause and effect. A heavy bag can cause back pain, and poor sitting habits have also been linked to low back pain. In our clinical experience, we see that one-sided habits such as always sitting at the desk leaning to one side or always carrying a bag on the same shoulder can make postural asymmetry and pain more noticeable in young people going through a growth spurt and those with flexible connective tissue; so we recommend sharing the load between both sides. This is a clinical observation, not a research finding.
tur32-29: Yes. According to the SRS, children with scoliosis can do any sport unless they have back pain; the international guideline (SOSORT) also recommends not giving up sport, even during brace treatment, because of its general health and psychological benefits. Contact or highly dynamic sports should be done with caution during bracing; if the risk of progression is high, talk to your doctor about competitive sport. No sport corrects a curve on its own.
tur32-30: Scoliosis-specific exercises can help prevent progression in small curves and slightly reduce the angle in some patients (differences are often within the measurement error); but they are not expected to remove the curve completely. According to the 2024 Cochrane review of 13 studies, the certainty of the evidence on the benefit of exercise is low or very low. The treatment needed is decided by considering the curve angle and growth status together.
tur32-31: The effect of a brace depends on how long it is worn. In the BrAIST study the brace was prescribed for at least 18 hours a day; in those who actually wore it for an average of 13 hours or more a day the success rate was 90–93%, while in those who wore it for less than 6 hours the result was no different from not wearing a brace. Your doctor decides the wearing time. In a Cochrane review of 7 studies and 662 adolescents, a rigid brace increased the success rate at 2 years compared with observation in curves of 20–40 degrees; all the studies showed that bracing prevented curve progression, but the quality of the evidence ranged from low to very low.
tur32-32: Not always. In growing young people whose curve is progressing beyond 45 degrees, surgery is usually recommended. In people who have finished growing, however, the decision is based not only on the angle but on whether the curve is progressing, trunk balance, pain, lung function and the person's expectations. In our clinical experience, we see that surgeons may recommend regular follow-up for some patients whose trunk is balanced, whose curve is not progressing and whose daily life is not restricted (this is a clinical observation, not a research finding). However, curves over 50 degrees at the end of growth usually continue to progress slowly in adulthood; regular X-ray checks are needed even when surgery is not recommended. You make the decision together with your spine surgeon.
tur32-33: Curves under 30 degrees usually either do not progress or progress very slowly. In a Danish study in which patients treated with a brace or observation were followed for an average of 41 years, curves increased by an average of 0.2–0.5 degrees per year in adulthood; even curves under 25 degrees increased by about 7 degrees on average over 40 years, and the differences between individuals were large. The authors recommend that people with a moderate curve at the end of growth have one more X-ray check in early adulthood.
tur32-34: Numbness or weakness in the arms or legs, walking difficulties
tur32-35: Sudden loss of bladder or bowel control, or rapidly increasing weakness in the legs: go to the emergency department the same day
